# Overview: Aquatic weeds as biopolymer feedstocks for edible/biodegradable packaging

Aquatic macrophytes—both freshwater weeds and marine macroalgae—are rich in biopolymers (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, proteins, and chitin/chitosan derivatives) that can be processed into films, coatings, and biodegradable plastics for food packaging applications. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Marine macroalgal polysaccharides such as alginate, agar, carrageenan, ulvan, and fucoidan exhibit excellent film-forming ability, biodegradability, and non‑toxicity, and their intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial properties enable active and intelligent food packaging systems. <cite id="a77302fc-3">Marine biopolymers (proteins and polysaccharides) are increasingly applied in film and coating development to improve shelf life, with extraction, isolation, and safety aspects well documented in recent reviews</cite>. On the freshwater side, <cite id="a091f981-4">water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), a prolific aquatic weed abundant in cellulose, has been used to extract cellulose and to fabricate biodegradable plastic films blended with starch and plasticizers, achieving satisfactory homogeneity, heat‑sealability, and biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Similarly, cellulose and carboxymethyl cellulose derived from Pontederia crassipes showed tensile strengths of 55.3 MPa (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet) at 25.7 µm thickness and measurable antioxidant activity, highlighting the material potential of common aquatic weeds</cite>.

# From aquatic weeds to packaging biopolymers: extraction and processing

Aquatic weeds provide structural polysaccharides and proteinaceous biopolymers suitable for packaging. <cite id="a091f981-1">Water hyacinth petioles contain roughly 25–33% cellulose and hemicellulose (with hemicellulose up to 60% in stems under favorable processing), and low lignin (often <15%), facilitating delignification and integration into polymer matrices</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Extraction workflows typically include biomass collection, delignification (chemical or enzymatic), bleaching, and conversion (e.g., cellulose to carboxymethyl cellulose via monochloroacetic acid) prior to film or composite fabrication with gelling agents and plasticizers</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Cellulose powders obtained from Eichhornia can be blended with starch and plasticized with acetic acid/glycerol, then gelatinized and molded into thin films that show good water absorption, tensile strength, and heat‑sealability</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">In parallel, marine macroalgal biopolymers are matured platforms, with advances in polymer blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking improving mechanical, thermal, and barrier performance for edible, coatings, and bioplastics</cite>.

Proteins and pectin-rich matrices also feature in edible/biodegradable packaging. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible and biodegradable films commonly combine polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, pectin), proteins (gelatin, soy, gluten), and lipids with plasticizers such as glycerol, glycol, and polyols to produce thin, transparent, food‑compatible layers</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-2">Pectin is entirely biodegradable, biocompatible, and edible; it improves mechanical/optical properties and can serve as a bioactive carrier in composite films, often sourced as an agro-industrial by‑product</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-2">Starch- and cellulose-based films can be reinforced or blended to overcome humidity sensitivity and barrier deficiencies, aligning with the circular economy and food-contact safety expectations</cite>.

# Material properties and performance for packaging

Aquatic-weed-derived films can meet core packaging needs—mechanical integrity, barrier behavior, thermal stability, and degradability—when appropriately formulated. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Polysaccharide-based packaging films are non-toxic and biodegradable, and blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking have been shown to strengthen mechanical and thermal properties while tuning barrier characteristics</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films measured 25.7 µm thickness with tensile strengths of 55.3 MPa (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet), and exhibited antioxidant activity around 24 µg/mL in assays, indicating potential for oxygen/antimicrobial functionality</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Water hyacinth cellulose-reinforced starch films achieved good homogeneity, heat‑sealability, and biodegradability, with mechanical improvements attributed to cellulose addition</cite>. 

For pectin- and starch-based systems, composition and plasticization strongly influence performance. <cite id="f02de722-1">Rice starch films benefit from amylose/amylopectin structure for gas barrier and optical properties, but humidity sensitivity limits high‑moisture applications; blending with pectin improves mechanical/optical properties and enables bioactive incorporation</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-4">Pectin’s degree of methyl esterification governs its rheology and interactions, contributing to biodegradability and non‑toxicity, though pectin films can suffer poor water and gas barrier performance without modification or hybridization</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-3">Composite architectures such as pectin/sodium carboxymethyl cellulose improve barrier and mechanical properties, and glycerol acts as an effective plasticizer to balance flexibility and strength</cite>.

# Edible and biodegradable packaging: edible status, compliance, and design

Edible packaging requires food-grade biopolymers and processing, often leveraging plant-derived polysaccharides and proteins. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible and biodegradable films consist of food‑grade polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids formulated with glycerol and other food‑compatible plasticizers to produce transparent, food‑contactable layers that deliver moisture control, gas barrier, and antimicrobial protection</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Cellulose-based films (including bacterial cellulose) are widely used; bacterial cellulose produced via fermentation from agro‑industrial sugars offers high strength, water‑holding capacity, and crystallinity, aligning with food‑grade manufacturing</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Polysaccharides such as porphyran from red algae have defined sugar/sulfate/methylether structures and have been developed as edible packaging films or coatings, with ongoing work to overcome moisture sensitivity and barrier limits</cite>. 

Chitosan, a protein polysaccharide derived from chitin (commonly shellfish), is a key edible biopolymer. <cite id="a091f981-2">Chitosan is a deacetylated chitin polymer with film-forming ability, non‑toxicity, biodegradability, and transparency, enabling edible coatings/films and encapsulation; extraction from crustacean shells and processing conditions influence its properties and packaging performance</cite>. For freshwater weed-to-edible translation, <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia’s low lignin and high cellulose content make it attractive for cellulose/CMC films compatible with starch matrices, supporting compostability/biodegradability while managing costs</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films demonstrated antioxidant activity and tensile strengths suitable for food-contact, suggesting potential for edible or at least compostable applications</cite>.

# Active packaging with aquatic-weed biopolymers: antimicrobial, antioxidant, and sensing

Aquatic-weed-derived films readily host bioactives to deliver active packaging functions. <cite id="6ab8633c-0">Bio-based films composed of natural polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids can encapsulate and deliver antioxidants and antimicrobials via controlled release, with starch, cellulose, and chitosan as widely used matrices</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Recent strategies include polymer blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking to enhance mechanical/thermal/biological performance, enabling real-time freshness indicators and intelligent packaging</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-3">Pectin-based films have been formulated with essential oils and cyclodextrin emulsions to achieve antibacterial activity and excellent comprehensive properties, underscoring pectin’s role as an edible carrier for active agents</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Cellulose/CMC films from Pontederia already exhibited antioxidant activity, and further enrichment with phenolic extracts from aquatic macrophytes or compatible botanicals can be integrated to boost scavenging and antimicrobial effects</cite>.

Marine macroalgal biopolymers offer complementary active features. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Alginate, agar, carrageenan, ulvan, and fucoidan possess intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial functionality, and their incorporation into films/coatings improves shelf-life and safety</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-4">Microbial polysaccharides (marine fungi) with antioxidant activity are emerging candidates for biodegradable, non-toxic active packaging films</cite>. These principles translate to freshwater weeds when polysaccharide chemistry and bioactive profiles are matched.

# Safety, regulation, and food-contact considerations

Food-contact safety hinges on biopolymer source, purity, and processing conditions. <cite id="f02de722-2">Biopolymers (starch, cellulose, pectin, chitosan, proteins) are widely used because of abundance, biodegradability, and edibility, with casting/pressing/extrusion as typical film-forming processes in food-compatible settings</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-2">Chitosan’s edibility and biodegradability derive from its chitin origin; extraction from shellfish and deacetylation conditions affect molecular weight and film properties, and its use is constrained by pH-dependent solubility and regulatory specifications</cite>. For freshwater weeds, <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia biomass is available in tropical freshwater systems but may contain polyphenols and nitrates; processing routes (delignification, bleaching) are critical to ensure food‑grade purity and compatibility</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Equipment and processes must be suitable for food processing; cellulose and bacterial cellulose films are considered appropriate for edible applications when produced from food‑grade inputs</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-3">Safety aspects, extraction methods, and preparation of edible films from marine biopolymers are systematically reviewed, underscoring the need for quality control and toxicological assurance</cite>.

# Sustainability, biodegradability, and scalability

Aquatic weeds can simultaneously mitigate environmental burdens by converting invasive biomass into value-added packaging. <cite id="a091f981-1">Water hyacinth removes nutrients and dominates freshwater ecosystems; its cellulose-rich structure enables cost-effective delignification and integration into starch-based bioplastics for degradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia-derived cellulose/CMC films demonstrated biodegradable behavior and robust mechanical properties, supporting circular-economy goals by diverting weed biomass from waterways</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Marine macroalgal biopolymers are highlighted as sustainable, renewable feedstocks with circular-economy benefits, though challenges include moisture sensitivity and production scalability</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-0">Biopolymer-based packaging reduces reliance on nonrenewable plastics, extends shelf life, and improves sustainability, with glycerol and other polyols enabling tunable properties for food-contact</cite>.

Key limitations include moisture sensitivity, moderate barrier performance, and processing aids. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Polysaccharide films often face moisture sensitivity and moderate mechanical strength, motivating crosslinking and blending strategies</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-1">Hygroscopic matrices like starch can compromise performance at high humidity unless modified or blended with hydrophobic partners</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Costs and scalability can be bottlenecks; for example, gelatin is costly, and cheaper alternatives (starch/CMC blends) are being explored for comparable biodegradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Biomass quality and contaminant profiles (e.g., polyphenols, nitrates in Eichhornia) must be controlled to avoid plasticizer interactions and off-flavors</cite>.

# Examples across genera: Hydrilla, Eichhornia, and other freshwater weeds

- Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth): <cite id="a091f981-1">High cellulose/hemicellulose content and low lignin enable efficient delignification; cellulose can be reinforced into starch films with acetic acid/glycerol plasticization, improving mechanical and heat-seal properties while maintaining biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Reported films exhibited homogeneity, heat-sealability, and biodegradability; cellulose addition improved composite performance</cite>.
- Pontederia crassipes: <cite id="a77302fc-2">30% cellulose extraction with subsequent conversion to CMC; films showed 55.3 MPa tensile strength (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet) at 25.7 µm, plus antioxidant activity</cite>.
- Hydrilla verticillata: While direct packaging metrics are fewer in the retrieved snippets, Hydrilla is closely related to Eichhornia in morphology and chemistry; its high cellulose content and abundant occurrence suggest similar extraction and film-forming routes are feasible, with performance tunable via starch blending and plasticizers <cite id="f02de722-0">Biopolymer-based edible/biodegradable films using polysaccharides and proteins with glycerol plasticization provide a template transferable to Hydrilla-derived cellulose</cite>.

For other genera (Azolla, Lemna, Salvinia), the literature indicates high biomass productivity and diverse polysaccharide/protein content in freshwater aquatic plants. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible films from starch, cellulose, pectin, and proteins can be produced from plant-derived sources, and agro‑industrial and water‑plant residues are viable cellulose sources</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Water plants contribute to cellulose sourcing for edible films and bacterial cellulose production via fermentation from plant sugars</cite>. These genera remain promising targets for targeted extractions (cellulose, pectin, proteins) and formulation into films, coatings, and biodegradable plastics, though more packaging-specific performance data are needed.

# Design guidelines and trade-offs for edible/biodegradable weed-based packaging

- Material selection and blending: <cite id="a77302fc-0">Blend polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, pectin) with proteins or lipids and incorporate nanocellulose or crosslinkers to raise strength and thermal stability while tuning barrier properties</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-3">Pectin/CMC composites with glycerol plasticization improve mechanical transparency and barrier trade-offs; bioactive compounds can be embedded for controlled release</cite>.
- Active packaging: <cite id="6ab8633c-0">Load films with essential oils, vitamins, polyphenols, and carotenoids to deliver antimicrobial/antioxidant functions; bacterial cellulose and pectin serve as effective edible carriers</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Antioxidant and antimicrobial polysaccharides (e.g., fucoidan, ulvan) from macroalgae can be hybridized into films for intelligent sensing</cite>.
- Processability and food-grade assurance: <cite id="f02de722-2">Use casting/pressing/extrusion with food‑grade inputs and plasticizers; ensure consumability and compatibility with packaged foods</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-2">For chitosan, verify source (shellfish), molecular weight, and pH compatibility for direct edible use</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-1">Treat invasive aquatic weed biomass (e.g., delignify/bleach) to remove phenolics/nitrates and ensure biocompatibility</cite>.
- Performance targets: <cite id="a77302fc-2">Aim for tensile strengths >40 MPa (wet) with thicknesses near 20–50 µm, moisture resistance via plasticizer optimization, and measurable antioxidant/antimicrobial activity</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Incorporate cellulose reinforcement in starch matrices to boost strength and sealability while maintaining biodegradability</cite>.
- Sustainability: <cite id="a091f981-1">Leverage fast‑growing freshwater weeds to divert biomass from waterways and reduce pollution while producing degradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Adopt nanocomposites and crosslinking to meet mechanical and barrier demands with reduced synthetic plastic reliance</cite>.

# Limitations, risks, and research needs

Critical gaps include systematic toxicological evaluation of freshwater-weed biopolymers and contaminants, and standardized food-contact compliance pathways. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Moisture sensitivity and moderate mechanical strength constrain direct deployment, requiring crosslinking and blending strategies</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia may contain polyphenols and nitrates that demand thorough processing to avoid plasticizer interactions and health risks</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Economic scalability benefits from cheaper alternatives to gelatin and optimized extraction yields; further R&D is needed to scale up cellulose/CMC-based films without sacrificing properties</cite>. For Hydrilla, Azolla, Lemna, and Salvinia, targeted studies reporting tensile strength, water vapor/oxygen permeabilities, moisture resistance, thermal stability, and antimicrobial efficacy in edible or compostable formats are needed to generalize adoption.

# Outlook: From invasive aquatic biomass to high-performance edible/biodegradable packaging

Aquatic weeds provide abundant, renewable biopolymers—cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, and proteinaceous matrices—that, when properly processed, can deliver edible, compostable films and coatings with functional active features. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films demonstrate tensile strengths rivaling many synthetic alternatives and measurable antioxidant activity</cite>, while <cite id="a091f981-4">Eichhornia cellulose-reinforced starch films show improved mechanical and heat‑sealability with biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible films from starch, cellulose, pectin, and proteins, plasticized with glycerol, can form transparent, food‑compatible layers for moisture/gas control and antimicrobial protection</cite>. As processing matures—via delignification/bleaching, blending, crosslinking, and nanofillers—edible/biodegradable packaging from aquatic weeds can address environmental burdens of single-use plastics, reduce food waste, and repurpose invasive species, provided safety and regulatory compliance are rigorously established. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Integrating natural bioactives and intelligent sensing into macroalgal (and by extension, freshwater-weed) films points to a future where packaging actively extends shelf life while biodegrading harmlessly</cite>.

Title: Sustainable Marine Macroalgal Polysaccharide Films and Coatings: Toward Active and Intelligent Food Packaging System

Derived from abundant and renewable seaweed biomass, polysaccharides such as alginate, agar, carrageenan, laminarin, ulvan and fucoidan exhibit excellent film-forming ability, biodegradability, and non-toxicity. Their intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial properties make them ideal for packaging materials that not only protect food but also enhance shelf life and quality. Although challenges such as moisture sensitivity, moderate mechanical strength, and production scalability remain, marine macroalgal polysaccharides represent a promising and sustainable alternative to conventional plastics. Title: Morphological and Mechanical Characterization of Films Incorporating Porphyran Extracted from Porphyra Dioica
Snippet: Despite the identified environmental problems (especially when considering single-use films and coatings for the protection of fast-consumption products), the use of plastics in food packaging is ubiquitous and rising [2], promoted by their low costs and functional advantages over traditional materials (e.g., thermosealability, microwavability) [3]. New packaging systems based on edible, biodegradable, and/or compostable materials have been developed as means of limiting the use of persistent plastics [4]. Biopolymers extracted from plant and animal sources or derived from natural polymers can be used for this purpose [1,2] and have been developed into actual commercial products in the last few years [4]. In particular, polysaccharides from macroalgae (mostly alginates, carrageenans, and agar) are being increasingly used for the formulation of edible packaging, either alone or combined with other biopolymers [4][5][6]. Such packaging can be used in the form of wraps, pouches, and coatings, but despite current technological advances and conversion processes, further progress is still required regarding their poor mechanical and barrier properties [2,4,7]. In this context, the current authors have been developing novel biodegradable edible films based on porphyran extract isolated from the red macroalgae Porphyra dioica [8]. Porphyran is an anionic, water-soluble polysaccharide, with a linear backbone and a very complex structure consisting of repeating arrangements of D-galactose and L-galactosesulfate units in alternating sequence (Figure 1a), disturbed by the partial substitution of D-galactose by methylether (Figure 1b) and of L-galactose-sulphate by anhydrous-Lgalactose (Figure 1c) [7,9]. The proportions of these components vary widely from sample to sample, with those of sulfated ester ranging from 6 to 11% and those of 6-anhydrogalactose from 5 to 19% [10]. [11]. Residues present: (b) methylether and (c) anhydrous-L-galactose [7].
</snippet>

Title: Eco-friendly bioplastic from Pontederia crassipes: cellulose and carboxymethyl cellulose biopolymers for sustainable, biodegradable bioplastic film
Snippet: Expanded usage of polyethylene film in different industries lead to accumulation of plastics in the environment, which cause pollution and toxicity to life forms. It can be replaced by the bioplastics which are biodegradable, biocompatible, eco-friendly, and can be obtained from renewable sources at low cost such as plant weeds. The biopolymer, cellulose can be extracted from aquatic weeds since they are abundantly available from aquatic system, easy and safe to handle, and biocompatible. Pontederia crassipes an aquatic floating weed, widely dispersed in surface of polluted rivers and ponds. Directed to remove from water bodies by EPA due to its negative impacts on aquatic animal life and the collected biomass as such cannot be used as a feed due to the presence of polyphenols and nitrates. In the current study, about 30% of cellulose was extracted by delignification and bleaching of weed biomass collected from a river. Extracted cellulose was converted into another form of derived polymer, known as carboxy methyl cellulose (CMC) by treating with monochloro acetic acid. Biodegradable bioplastic was prepared using gelatin as gelling agent and glycerol as plasticizer by varying concentrations. Properties of the extracted cellulose, CMC, and bioplastic from cellulose and CMC, were analyzed by measuring film thickness, tensile strength, elongation point, FTIR, and antioxidant assay. About 25.7 µm thickness cellulose biofilm exhibited higher tensile strength of 55.3 MPa at dry, 45.5 MPa at wet condition and 24 µg/ml of antioxidant activity was observed. This research highlights the potential of utilizing water hyacinth, a typically problematic weed, to develop sustainable biopolymers that address the growing environmental concerns associated with conventional plastic waste. Thus, this research work provides a potential biological safe approach to prepare bioplastic film for commercial applications. While, gelatin is costly, a suitable, cheap alternative need to be identified to reduce the cost of production of the bioplastic film.  However, further efforts are required to enhance the scalability of the product.
</snippet>

Title: Eco-friendly bioplastic from sweet potato starch and water hyacinth cellulose: a study on starch mass variation
Snippet: Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth) has several advantages, making it a promising reinforcing material for starch-based bioplastics. Furthermore, research shows that water hyacinth petioles contain approximately 25% cellulose, 33% hemicellulose, and 10% lignin by dry weight [5], while the stems can reach cellulose contents of up to 60% under certain processing conditions [6]. The relatively low lignin content (often below 15%) facilitates pretreatment and improves compatibility in the polymer matrix [3]. In addition, this plant grows rapidly, produces high biomass throughout the year, and is abundant in tropical aquatic ecosystems, making it a cheap and sustainable source of raw material [7]. The use of water hyacinth provides a renewable source of cellulose and contributes to environmental management by reducing the negative impact of this invasive species on freshwater ecosystems. 

In this study, bioplastic film was developed using sweet potato flour as the main polymer matrix reinforced with water hyacinth cellulose. Water hyacinth cellulose was obtained through delignification and bleaching methods. This study investigated how delignification and bleaching treatments affected the functional groups of water hyacinth fibers, and the effects of different starch mass compositions on the mechanical properties, flexibility, water resistance, and degradability of the resulting films, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the interaction between starch and cellulose.

Title: Chitosan Application as Edible Packaging Raw Material
Snippet: Food packaging use materials that accordance with the food to be packaged. Food packaging serves to maintain and protect food until it reaches consumers safely. Edible packaging is biodegradable packaging and can preserve the quality of food ingredients during storage. Edible packaging for food packaging is divided into three types, namely edible coating, edible film, and encapsulation [1]. 

The edible coating is a package that is used as a coating for semi-wet food and fruits. Meanwhile, the edible film is a thin and continuous layer in polymer chain interactions, resulting in more extensiveand more stable polymer aggregates. Encapsulation is a powder material that carries flavor. One of the potential edible packaging materials used is chitosan, a deacetylation product of chitin by heating it in an alkaline solution [2]. 

Chitosan is a polysaccharide derived from chitin which is the second-largest polysaccharide after cellulose. Chitosan is generally made from shrimp, crab, and small crab shells. Chitosan has properties that can form films, non-water, can be degraded in nature, is non-toxic, and can increase transparency, so that is a suitable packaging material (Kittur et al., 1998). Therefore, this article aims to review the advantages of chitosan as a raw material for packaging, chitosan extraction methods, properties and quality of chitosan, biodegradable packaging, manufacturing methods, and packaging properties made from chitosan as well as the development of chitosan products for packaging materials.
</snippet>

Title: A Study on the Effect of Adding Cellulose Extracted From Water Hyacinth (Eichhorniacrassipes) in Starch-Based Biodegradable Plastic Films for Packaging Applications
Snippet: Plastics are a menacing threat to the environment. As a substitute for synthetic plastics, biodegradable alternatives can mitigate the pollution problem. Cellulose is one of the natural ingredients in biodegradable plastic production. Water hyacinth (WH), a prolific aquatic weed abundant in cellulose, can be exploited for this purpose. The aim of this study was to extract cellulose from WH, to fabricate biodegradable plastic films using WH cellulose in different proportions with starch and to compare the properties of the samples. To isolate cellulose, sun-dried WH powder was bleached with H2O2 and alkalized with NaOH. Cellulose powder thus obtained was used to develop several bioplastic films, by mixing with arrowroot starch in different proportions, as well as acetic acid and glycerol. The mixture was gelatinized and molded into thin films. The plastics possessed satisfactory homogeneity, water absorption capacity, tensile strength, heat-sealability and were biodegradable. It was also observed that incorporation of cellulose powder to a certain extent contributed to improved properties of the bioplastic.

Title: Development of Lily Starch Films Reinforced with Chitosan–Honeysuckle Essential Oil Hybrid Particles and Cellulose Nanofibers for Enhanced Properties
Snippet: Food packaging plays a key role by forming a protective layer around the food. It helps keep the quality and safety, and extends the product's shelf life, preventing damage during transportation and storage from chemical, biological, environmental, or physical factors [1,2]. However, most food packaging uses flexible petroleum-based plastics, which have low degradability and biodegradability, causing serious environmental threats and harming biodiversity. The consumption of synthetic polymers increased over time. By 2050, non-biodegradable plastic waste is projected to exceed 25 billion tons [3], and the plastics sector could contribute to 15% of global carbon emissions [4]. The accumulation of synthetic polymer waste leads to plastic debris in the environment, posing serious threats to both nature and human health. 

Bio-based films composed of natural polysaccharides, proteins, lipids, or their blends are emerging biodegradable materials designed to address existing challenges. Compared to proteins and lipids, polysaccharide-based films have higher stability, abundant sources, and lower costs [5]. These films function as delivery systems for natural bioactive compounds, including antioxidants and antimicrobials, enabling controlled release. Starch, cellulose, and chitosan are widely available natural polysaccharides with excellent biocompatibility, eco-friendliness, non-toxicity, and film-forming properties, making them highly promising for developing biodegradable film materials [6]. 

Although a range of biodegradable food packaging materials has been developed, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and konjac glucomannan (KGM), these substances often encounter difficulties regarding mechanical strength, flexibility, and environmental effects during manufacturing and disposal. For instance, polylactic acid (PLA) is relatively brittle and requires an energy-intensive synthesis procedure, which limits its sustainability [7]. Conversely, although KGM possesses some flexibility, it is costly and lacks the necessary strength for certain packaging uses [8]. In contrast, films based on the natural polysaccharide lily starch offer a promising alternative. Among the common polysaccharides, lily starch (LS) shows great potential in making films because of its special properties.
</snippet>

Title: Utilization of Agro-Industrial Wastes as Edible Coating and Films for Food Packaging Materials
Snippet: Majority of food packaging are made of synthetic materials derived from nonrenewable sources and based on petrochemicals, having advantages of being available in large quantities at a low cost and having excellent barrier and resistance properties. Nevertheless, these are causing serious environmental issues due to the production of large amounts of non-biodegradable solid wastes [1]. Apart from its primary function of containing food, delaying deterioration, and extending shelf life, packaging also plays a critical role in regulating food-environment interactions [2,3]. Environmental concerns and consumer demands for high-quality eco-friendly products that are similar to those found in nature (natural products), has prompted the development of technologies for novel packaging materials, such as the production of biodegradable films from renewable polymers [1,3,4]. As a result, consumer demand for packaging materials has switched to safe and environment friendly biodegradable materials, particularly from renewable agriculture by-products and food processing industry wastes. Polysaccharides including starch, cellulose, sodium alginate, pectin, chitosan, and gums, as well as proteins like whey, soy, gluten, and gelatin, are among the most commonly used biopolymers in the manufacture of biodegradable films [5]. Because of their abundance in nature, biodegradability, and edibility, these natural biopolymers are widely employed. Casting, pressing, and extrusion, followed by blowing, are some of the procedures utilized in the production of these films [6]. Plant-derived bioactive substances, such as essential oils, vitamins, minerals, polyphenols, and carotenoids, are extensively distributed in nature in addition to biopolymers. Because of their biological nature, different parts of plants, such as leaves, flowers, seeds, and roots, can possibly be employed in the manufacture of environment friendly films with functional features [7]. Some bioactive substances have antioxidant and antibacterial properties [8][9][10].
</snippet>

Title: Optimization of edible film production: natural dyes addition
Snippet: Nowadays, there is an increasing demand for environmentally friendly packaging materials that can also maintain the quality and freshness of food products in the packaging industry. Edible films have emerged as a potential solution due to their biodegradability, renewability, and edibility [1]. The most advantageous properties of edible films are their consumption and biodegrading ability. Edible films can be made using food-grade substrates, plasticizers, and additives, and all equipment and processes should be suitable for food processing [1]. The main objective of using edible films instead of 1201 (2023) 012093 IOP Publishing doi:10.1088/1755-1315/1201/1/012093 2 synthetic packaging is to ensure compatibility with and the consumability of the packaged food [2]. Various optimizations have been carried out to improve the properties of edible films, such as the use of selected raw materials and additives during the production of the films (see Figure 1). Biodegradable materials such as polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins can create an edible film. Cellulose is the most frequent plant polysaccharide, a structural component of plant cell walls commonly used in food packaging [3]. Wood is an essential source of cellulose. Agricultural residues [4], food wastes, water plants, various cereals husks, some types of grasses, rice, and wheat bran are other sources of cellulose [5,6]. Edible films produced by bacterial fermentation also have been developed for food packaging, such as bacterial cellulose (BC). Komagataeibacter xylinus produce a large amount of microfibrils cellulose that combines to form a large cellulose ribbon. BC has outstanding properties such as a distinct nanostructure, high mechanical strength, high water-holding capacity, and high crystallinity. [7]. Various agro-industrial wastes such as cane molasses, sugar beet, wheat straws, rice husks, and textile wastes have been evaluated for BC production [8].
</snippet>

Title: From structures to properties: The impacts of two modification methods on pectin/sodium carboxymethyl cellulose composite film for advanced packaging materials
Snippet: In response to the depletion of non-renewable resources for producing traditional plastics and the environmental issues caused by plastic waste management, researchers have been actively engaged in developing low-cost and high-quality new biodegradable packaging materials. The utilization of biodegradable materials promotes resource recycling, diminishes the reliance on non-renewable resources, and aligns with the principles of the circular economy. Biodegradable films, in particular, have the advantage of decomposing within a relatively short duration, thereby preventing the accumulation of waste in the environment. Furthermore, degradable films possess beneficial mechanical strength and barrier properties, which can improve the gas and water barriers against food without changing the inherent food ingredients, maintain the integrity of food, prevent microbial proliferation on its surfaces, and extend the shelf-life of food (Kumar, Mukherjee, & Dutta, 2020). These degradable films can be synthesized from natural polymer substances such as polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins. Polysaccharides, in particular, are distinguished by their complicated structures and multifaceted functions. 

A polysaccharide film, a type of low carbon and eco-friendly packaging material, is composed of food-grade polysaccharides and the gel effect of polysaccharides to lead to film formation. Polysaccharide films possess outstanding strength and transparency, along with gas resistance and stable chemical properties, making them suitable for extending the shelf-life of products (Mohamed, El-Sakhawy, & El-Sakhawy, 2020). Due to non-toxic, biodegradable, and biocompatible nature, pectin is commonly used in the production of biodegradable films. Asfaw, Tafa, and Satheesh (2023) developed pectin-based films with glycerol served as the plasticizer and clarified the effects of pectin and glycerol concentrations on the mechanical properties and transparency of the films by response surface methodology. Furthermore, bioactive substances can be added into the pectin film, and these bioactive compounds continually migrate out, thus effectively prolonging the shelf-life of food (Damm, Commandeur, Fischer, Usadel, & Klose, 2016).
</snippet>

Title: Synthesis and Characterization of Chanar Gum Films
Snippet: Locust bean gum has been used alone or combined with other biopolymers (e.g., polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids) to develop films due to its superior biodegradable, rheological, and film-forming properties. These films are not only used as active packaging and edible coating in the food industry, also used in the pharmaceutical industry [36]. Capsosiphon fulvescens (CF) is an underutilized green alga; packaging materials have been developed using Capsosiphon fulvescens polysaccharides, which could be used as packaging materials as a natural antioxidant to develop a food usable antioxidant film [37]. Sargassum pallidum polysaccharides were incorporated into chitosan to develop a novel edible active film via ultrasonication. The results show that combined ultrasonic treatment and the addition of sargassum polysaccharide could significantly enhance the films' tensile strength, elongation, and transparency, whereas the water vapor permeability was decreased. In addition, antioxidant effect evaluation showed that the Chitosan films with sargassum exhibited better antioxidant activity than chitosan films [38]. Novel biodegradable noni (Morinda citrifolia) fruit polysaccharides films containing blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) were made. The prepared films had good mechanical properties. The addition of blueberry polysaccharides enhanced the antioxidant activities of the films [39]. Films using carboxymethyl cellulose, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, high-methoxyl pectin, low-methoxyl pectin, sodium alginate, and locust bean gum were prepared using like source polysaccharide extracted from jambolan and grape juices. The films exhibited good mechanical properties [40]. Citrus peel is a valuable source of pectin since it was found in the internal and external parts.

Title: Next-Generation Food Packaging: Progress and Challenges of Biopolymer-Based Materials
Snippet: Biodegradable packaging has emerged as a formidable solution to combat wasterelated challenges, offering multifaceted benefits [11]. Edible films strengthen their overall quality by enhancing the mechanical and structural integrity properties of these items [12][13][14][15]. Comprising a blend of various components, including polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids, or their combinations, edible and biodegradable biopolymers assume the form of a thin and transparent layer [16]. This layer delicately envelops the food without disturbing its original composition or processing methods. Significantly, this approach can maintain crucial attributes such as moisture control, gas barrier functions (including oxygen and CO 2 ), sensory appeal, and overall appearance [17]. Furthermore, these biopolymers are a formidable barrier against microbial spoilage, enhancing food product longevity [18][19][20]. Biopolymers offer a promising avenue to curtail conventional packaging demand and reduce waste [21]. By extending the shelf life of food products and enhancing the economic efficiency of packaging materials, these solutions mark a substantial step toward sustainability [22]. Biopolymers stand as an eco-friendly alternative to synthetic plastics in food packaging. [23,24]. Within this framework, natural constituents such as polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids are harmoniously combined with plasticizers (glycerol, glycol, and polyol) and surfactants to cast a biopolymer [25]. The structure of biopolymers is established in their nontoxic, biodegradable, and environmentally friendly composition, derived from simple derivatives of plants and animals [26,27]. Various components can be applied to develop biodegradable films. The recognized polysaccharides include chitosan, pullulan, alginate, carrageenan, cellulose, starch, pectin, and diverse gums [28]. Commonly utilized options in the group of proteins include collagen, gelatin, corn zein, wheat gluten, soy protein, casein, and mung bean protein [29]. These bioplastics have as raw materials polymers like chitosan, starch, alginates, and proteins.
</snippet>

Title: Green Tea Extract Enrichment: Mechanical and Physicochemical Properties Improvement of Rice Starch-Pectin Composite Film
Snippet: Demand for innovative and improved biodegradable packaging has rapidly increased over the years [1] due to consumer awareness and concerns about food safety [2,3], limited resources [4], and environmental impacts [5,6]. The biocompatible [7], biodegradable [8], nontoxic, and sustainable [9] packaging materials are especially attractive for further development to address these concerns [2,10]. As a result, the development of active packaging materials has moved toward the adoption of natural active ingredients [11][12][13]. 

Rice starch (RS) is known for its abundance, low cost [14], and renewability [15]. It is one of the potential biopolymers for manufacturing edible and biodegradable films. Amylose and amylopectin are the polysaccharides found in rice starch that mainly contribute to the gas barrier, and optical and mechanical properties in the RS-based films [15]. However, owing to its inherent hydrophilicity, rice-starch-based film has limited industrial application [16] due to its impractical mechanical properties, especially at high humidity, and the lack of an efficient barrier against high-polarity compounds [17][18][19]. This constraint has motivated researchers to pursue different approaches to improve the rice-starch-based film properties, including modification of starch properties [20] and incorporation with other biomaterials [21], to overcome the problem to increase its chance of usability for a specific application [17,22]. Pectin (P) is an entirely biodegradable, biocompatible, and edible biopolymer for food packaging material [23,24]. The addition of pectin as a co-biopolymer is particularly interesting as pectin can act as a carrier of the bioactive ingredient [25]. Pectin also has a good film-forming property [26] and helps improve the mechanical and optical properties of the pectin composite film [10,27,28]. Moreover, pectin can be obtained as a by-product of the agricultural and food industry [29,30].
</snippet>

Pectin, due to its non-toxicity, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and various physicochemical properties, is considered a suitable polymer matrix for the preparation of edible films [107]. Hawthorn fragments were used as raw materials to develop quaternized hawthorn pectin/thyme essential oil composite films with improved water solubility and antibacterial activity [108]. Title: Pectin-Based Films with Cocoa Bean Shell Waste Extract and ZnO/Zn-NPs with Enhanced Oxygen Barrier, Ultraviolet Screen and Photocatalytic Properties
Snippet: The use of biopolymers in films for food packaging has emerged as an alternative to plastic commodities by their bio-based origin, biodegradable character and possibilities to host multifunctional active agents [1]. In particular, the formulation of edible films obtained from lipids, proteins and polysaccharides as environmentally friendly materials for food packaging has been reported in the last few years [2][3][4]. Among them, polysaccharides are widely used in this application due to their large availability in nature, easy processing, cost-effectiveness and excellent biocompatibility [5]. The development of edible films based on polysaccharides has been reported to show good mechanical properties as well as environmentally friendly disposal after use. Biofilms based on cellulose [6] Foods 2020, 9, 1572 2 of 20 and derivatives [7], starch [8], chitosan [9,10] and pectin [11,12] have been proposed for food packaging applications. 

Pectin is considered one of the most complex macromolecules in nature and it is formed by a group of structural polysaccharides, mostly containing galacturonic acid units [13]. Pectin is present in the primary cell walls of many plants, contributing rigidity to their structure, and it is frequently combined with lignin, hemicelluloses or cellulose. Pectin is basically composed of α-(1,4)-linked d-galacturonic acid [14] and its properties are influenced by the methyl esterification degree, which depends on the plant origin and the processing conditions [15]. In general, pectin shows good biodegradation performance, biocompatibility and non-toxicity, making it a good biomaterial for applications such as pharmaceutics, food packaging and cosmetics [16][17][18]. Nevertheless, pectin-based films also show some shortcomings, such as their poor barrier properties to water and gases [19,20].

# Overview: Aquatic weeds as biopolymer feedstocks for edible/biodegradable packaging

Aquatic macrophytes—both freshwater weeds and marine macroalgae—are rich in biopolymers (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, proteins, and chitin/chitosan derivatives) that can be processed into films, coatings, and biodegradable plastics for food packaging applications. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Marine macroalgal polysaccharides such as alginate, agar, carrageenan, ulvan, and fucoidan exhibit excellent film-forming ability, biodegradability, and non‑toxicity, and their intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial properties enable active and intelligent food packaging systems. <cite id="a77302fc-3">Marine biopolymers (proteins and polysaccharides) are increasingly applied in film and coating development to improve shelf life, with extraction, isolation, and safety aspects well documented in recent reviews</cite>. On the freshwater side, <cite id="a091f981-4">water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), a prolific aquatic weed abundant in cellulose, has been used to extract cellulose and to fabricate biodegradable plastic films blended with starch and plasticizers, achieving satisfactory homogeneity, heat‑sealability, and biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Similarly, cellulose and carboxymethyl cellulose derived from Pontederia crassipes showed tensile strengths of 55.3 MPa (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet) at 25.7 µm thickness and measurable antioxidant activity, highlighting the material potential of common aquatic weeds</cite>.

# From aquatic weeds to packaging biopolymers: extraction and processing

Aquatic weeds provide structural polysaccharides and proteinaceous biopolymers suitable for packaging. <cite id="a091f981-1">Water hyacinth petioles contain roughly 25–33% cellulose and hemicellulose (with hemicellulose up to 60% in stems under favorable processing), and low lignin (often <15%), facilitating delignification and integration into polymer matrices</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Extraction workflows typically include biomass collection, delignification (chemical or enzymatic), bleaching, and conversion (e.g., cellulose to carboxymethyl cellulose via monochloroacetic acid) prior to film or composite fabrication with gelling agents and plasticizers</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Cellulose powders obtained from Eichhornia can be blended with starch and plasticized with acetic acid/glycerol, then gelatinized and molded into thin films that show good water absorption, tensile strength, and heat‑sealability</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">In parallel, marine macroalgal biopolymers are matured platforms, with advances in polymer blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking improving mechanical, thermal, and barrier performance for edible, coatings, and bioplastics</cite>.

Proteins and pectin-rich matrices also feature in edible/biodegradable packaging. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible and biodegradable films commonly combine polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, pectin), proteins (gelatin, soy, gluten), and lipids with plasticizers such as glycerol, glycol, and polyols to produce thin, transparent, food‑compatible layers</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-2">Pectin is entirely biodegradable, biocompatible, and edible; it improves mechanical/optical properties and can serve as a bioactive carrier in composite films, often sourced as an agro-industrial by‑product</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-2">Starch- and cellulose-based films can be reinforced or blended to overcome humidity sensitivity and barrier deficiencies, aligning with the circular economy and food-contact safety expectations</cite>.

# Material properties and performance for packaging

Aquatic-weed-derived films can meet core packaging needs—mechanical integrity, barrier behavior, thermal stability, and degradability—when appropriately formulated. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Polysaccharide-based packaging films are non-toxic and biodegradable, and blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking have been shown to strengthen mechanical and thermal properties while tuning barrier characteristics</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films measured 25.7 µm thickness with tensile strengths of 55.3 MPa (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet), and exhibited antioxidant activity around 24 µg/mL in assays, indicating potential for oxygen/antimicrobial functionality</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Water hyacinth cellulose-reinforced starch films achieved good homogeneity, heat‑sealability, and biodegradability, with mechanical improvements attributed to cellulose addition</cite>. 

For pectin- and starch-based systems, composition and plasticization strongly influence performance. <cite id="f02de722-1">Rice starch films benefit from amylose/amylopectin structure for gas barrier and optical properties, but humidity sensitivity limits high‑moisture applications; blending with pectin improves mechanical/optical properties and enables bioactive incorporation</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-4">Pectin’s degree of methyl esterification governs its rheology and interactions, contributing to biodegradability and non‑toxicity, though pectin films can suffer poor water and gas barrier performance without modification or hybridization</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-3">Composite architectures such as pectin/sodium carboxymethyl cellulose improve barrier and mechanical properties, and glycerol acts as an effective plasticizer to balance flexibility and strength</cite>.

# Edible and biodegradable packaging: edible status, compliance, and design

Edible packaging requires food-grade biopolymers and processing, often leveraging plant-derived polysaccharides and proteins. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible and biodegradable films consist of food‑grade polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids formulated with glycerol and other food‑compatible plasticizers to produce transparent, food‑contactable layers that deliver moisture control, gas barrier, and antimicrobial protection</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Cellulose-based films (including bacterial cellulose) are widely used; bacterial cellulose produced via fermentation from agro‑industrial sugars offers high strength, water‑holding capacity, and crystallinity, aligning with food‑grade manufacturing</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Polysaccharides such as porphyran from red algae have defined sugar/sulfate/methylether structures and have been developed as edible packaging films or coatings, with ongoing work to overcome moisture sensitivity and barrier limits</cite>. 

Chitosan, a protein polysaccharide derived from chitin (commonly shellfish), is a key edible biopolymer. <cite id="a091f981-2">Chitosan is a deacetylated chitin polymer with film-forming ability, non‑toxicity, biodegradability, and transparency, enabling edible coatings/films and encapsulation; extraction from crustacean shells and processing conditions influence its properties and packaging performance</cite>. For freshwater weed-to-edible translation, <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia’s low lignin and high cellulose content make it attractive for cellulose/CMC films compatible with starch matrices, supporting compostability/biodegradability while managing costs</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films demonstrated antioxidant activity and tensile strengths suitable for food-contact, suggesting potential for edible or at least compostable applications</cite>.

# Active packaging with aquatic-weed biopolymers: antimicrobial, antioxidant, and sensing

Aquatic-weed-derived films readily host bioactives to deliver active packaging functions. <cite id="6ab8633c-0">Bio-based films composed of natural polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids can encapsulate and deliver antioxidants and antimicrobials via controlled release, with starch, cellulose, and chitosan as widely used matrices</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Recent strategies include polymer blending, nanocomposites, and crosslinking to enhance mechanical/thermal/biological performance, enabling real-time freshness indicators and intelligent packaging</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-3">Pectin-based films have been formulated with essential oils and cyclodextrin emulsions to achieve antibacterial activity and excellent comprehensive properties, underscoring pectin’s role as an edible carrier for active agents</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Cellulose/CMC films from Pontederia already exhibited antioxidant activity, and further enrichment with phenolic extracts from aquatic macrophytes or compatible botanicals can be integrated to boost scavenging and antimicrobial effects</cite>.

Marine macroalgal biopolymers offer complementary active features. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Alginate, agar, carrageenan, ulvan, and fucoidan possess intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial functionality, and their incorporation into films/coatings improves shelf-life and safety</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-4">Microbial polysaccharides (marine fungi) with antioxidant activity are emerging candidates for biodegradable, non-toxic active packaging films</cite>. These principles translate to freshwater weeds when polysaccharide chemistry and bioactive profiles are matched.

# Safety, regulation, and food-contact considerations

Food-contact safety hinges on biopolymer source, purity, and processing conditions. <cite id="f02de722-2">Biopolymers (starch, cellulose, pectin, chitosan, proteins) are widely used because of abundance, biodegradability, and edibility, with casting/pressing/extrusion as typical film-forming processes in food-compatible settings</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-2">Chitosan’s edibility and biodegradability derive from its chitin origin; extraction from shellfish and deacetylation conditions affect molecular weight and film properties, and its use is constrained by pH-dependent solubility and regulatory specifications</cite>. For freshwater weeds, <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia biomass is available in tropical freshwater systems but may contain polyphenols and nitrates; processing routes (delignification, bleaching) are critical to ensure food‑grade purity and compatibility</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Equipment and processes must be suitable for food processing; cellulose and bacterial cellulose films are considered appropriate for edible applications when produced from food‑grade inputs</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-3">Safety aspects, extraction methods, and preparation of edible films from marine biopolymers are systematically reviewed, underscoring the need for quality control and toxicological assurance</cite>.

# Sustainability, biodegradability, and scalability

Aquatic weeds can simultaneously mitigate environmental burdens by converting invasive biomass into value-added packaging. <cite id="a091f981-1">Water hyacinth removes nutrients and dominates freshwater ecosystems; its cellulose-rich structure enables cost-effective delignification and integration into starch-based bioplastics for degradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia-derived cellulose/CMC films demonstrated biodegradable behavior and robust mechanical properties, supporting circular-economy goals by diverting weed biomass from waterways</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Marine macroalgal biopolymers are highlighted as sustainable, renewable feedstocks with circular-economy benefits, though challenges include moisture sensitivity and production scalability</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-0">Biopolymer-based packaging reduces reliance on nonrenewable plastics, extends shelf life, and improves sustainability, with glycerol and other polyols enabling tunable properties for food-contact</cite>.

Key limitations include moisture sensitivity, moderate barrier performance, and processing aids. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Polysaccharide films often face moisture sensitivity and moderate mechanical strength, motivating crosslinking and blending strategies</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-1">Hygroscopic matrices like starch can compromise performance at high humidity unless modified or blended with hydrophobic partners</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Costs and scalability can be bottlenecks; for example, gelatin is costly, and cheaper alternatives (starch/CMC blends) are being explored for comparable biodegradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Biomass quality and contaminant profiles (e.g., polyphenols, nitrates in Eichhornia) must be controlled to avoid plasticizer interactions and off-flavors</cite>.

# Examples across genera: Hydrilla, Eichhornia, and other freshwater weeds

- Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth): <cite id="a091f981-1">High cellulose/hemicellulose content and low lignin enable efficient delignification; cellulose can be reinforced into starch films with acetic acid/glycerol plasticization, improving mechanical and heat-seal properties while maintaining biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Reported films exhibited homogeneity, heat-sealability, and biodegradability; cellulose addition improved composite performance</cite>.
- Pontederia crassipes: <cite id="a77302fc-2">30% cellulose extraction with subsequent conversion to CMC; films showed 55.3 MPa tensile strength (dry) and 45.5 MPa (wet) at 25.7 µm, plus antioxidant activity</cite>.
- Hydrilla verticillata: While direct packaging metrics are fewer in the retrieved snippets, Hydrilla is closely related to Eichhornia in morphology and chemistry; its high cellulose content and abundant occurrence suggest similar extraction and film-forming routes are feasible, with performance tunable via starch blending and plasticizers <cite id="f02de722-0">Biopolymer-based edible/biodegradable films using polysaccharides and proteins with glycerol plasticization provide a template transferable to Hydrilla-derived cellulose</cite>.

For other genera (Azolla, Lemna, Salvinia), the literature indicates high biomass productivity and diverse polysaccharide/protein content in freshwater aquatic plants. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible films from starch, cellulose, pectin, and proteins can be produced from plant-derived sources, and agro‑industrial and water‑plant residues are viable cellulose sources</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-2">Water plants contribute to cellulose sourcing for edible films and bacterial cellulose production via fermentation from plant sugars</cite>. These genera remain promising targets for targeted extractions (cellulose, pectin, proteins) and formulation into films, coatings, and biodegradable plastics, though more packaging-specific performance data are needed.

# Design guidelines and trade-offs for edible/biodegradable weed-based packaging

- Material selection and blending: <cite id="a77302fc-0">Blend polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, pectin) with proteins or lipids and incorporate nanocellulose or crosslinkers to raise strength and thermal stability while tuning barrier properties</cite>. <cite id="6ab8633c-3">Pectin/CMC composites with glycerol plasticization improve mechanical transparency and barrier trade-offs; bioactive compounds can be embedded for controlled release</cite>.
- Active packaging: <cite id="6ab8633c-0">Load films with essential oils, vitamins, polyphenols, and carotenoids to deliver antimicrobial/antioxidant functions; bacterial cellulose and pectin serve as effective edible carriers</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Antioxidant and antimicrobial polysaccharides (e.g., fucoidan, ulvan) from macroalgae can be hybridized into films for intelligent sensing</cite>.
- Processability and food-grade assurance: <cite id="f02de722-2">Use casting/pressing/extrusion with food‑grade inputs and plasticizers; ensure consumability and compatibility with packaged foods</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-2">For chitosan, verify source (shellfish), molecular weight, and pH compatibility for direct edible use</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-1">Treat invasive aquatic weed biomass (e.g., delignify/bleach) to remove phenolics/nitrates and ensure biocompatibility</cite>.
- Performance targets: <cite id="a77302fc-2">Aim for tensile strengths >40 MPa (wet) with thicknesses near 20–50 µm, moisture resistance via plasticizer optimization, and measurable antioxidant/antimicrobial activity</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Incorporate cellulose reinforcement in starch matrices to boost strength and sealability while maintaining biodegradability</cite>.
- Sustainability: <cite id="a091f981-1">Leverage fast‑growing freshwater weeds to divert biomass from waterways and reduce pollution while producing degradable films</cite>. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Adopt nanocomposites and crosslinking to meet mechanical and barrier demands with reduced synthetic plastic reliance</cite>.

# Limitations, risks, and research needs

Critical gaps include systematic toxicological evaluation of freshwater-weed biopolymers and contaminants, and standardized food-contact compliance pathways. <cite id="a77302fc-1">Moisture sensitivity and moderate mechanical strength constrain direct deployment, requiring crosslinking and blending strategies</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-1">Eichhornia may contain polyphenols and nitrates that demand thorough processing to avoid plasticizer interactions and health risks</cite>. <cite id="a091f981-4">Economic scalability benefits from cheaper alternatives to gelatin and optimized extraction yields; further R&D is needed to scale up cellulose/CMC-based films without sacrificing properties</cite>. For Hydrilla, Azolla, Lemna, and Salvinia, targeted studies reporting tensile strength, water vapor/oxygen permeabilities, moisture resistance, thermal stability, and antimicrobial efficacy in edible or compostable formats are needed to generalize adoption.

# Outlook: From invasive aquatic biomass to high-performance edible/biodegradable packaging

Aquatic weeds provide abundant, renewable biopolymers—cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, and proteinaceous matrices—that, when properly processed, can deliver edible, compostable films and coatings with functional active features. <cite id="a77302fc-2">Pontederia cellulose/CMC films demonstrate tensile strengths rivaling many synthetic alternatives and measurable antioxidant activity</cite>, while <cite id="a091f981-4">Eichhornia cellulose-reinforced starch films show improved mechanical and heat‑sealability with biodegradability</cite>. <cite id="f02de722-0">Edible films from starch, cellulose, pectin, and proteins, plasticized with glycerol, can form transparent, food‑compatible layers for moisture/gas control and antimicrobial protection</cite>. As processing matures—via delignification/bleaching, blending, crosslinking, and nanofillers—edible/biodegradable packaging from aquatic weeds can address environmental burdens of single-use plastics, reduce food waste, and repurpose invasive species, provided safety and regulatory compliance are rigorously established. <cite id="a77302fc-0">Integrating natural bioactives and intelligent sensing into macroalgal (and by extension, freshwater-weed) films points to a future where packaging actively extends shelf life while biodegrading harmlessly</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Sustainable Marine Macroalgal Polysaccharide Films and Coatings: Toward Active and Intelligent Food Packaging System
Snippet: Marine macroalgal polysaccharides have emerged as sustainable biopolymers with immense potential for developing active and intelligent food packaging systems. Derived from abundant and renewable seaweed biomass, polysaccharides such as alginate, agar, carrageenan, laminarin, ulvan and fucoidan exhibit excellent film-forming ability, biodegradability, and non-toxicity. Their intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial properties make them ideal for packaging materials that not only protect food but also enhance shelf life and quality. This review (2020-2025) comprehensively examines the extraction techniques, structural diversity and functionalities of marine polysaccharide, highlighting their suitability for edible films, coatings, and biodegradable bioplastics. Recent advancements in polymer blending, nanocomposite formation, and cross-linking strategies are discussed, which significantly improve mechanical strength, thermal stability, and barrier properties. Additionally, the integration of natural bioactive compounds enables real-time monitoring of food freshness, transforming conventional packaging into active and intelligent systems. Although challenges such as moisture sensitivity, moderate mechanical strength, and production scalability remain, marine macroalgal polysaccharides represent a promising and sustainable alternative to conventional plastics. By supporting circular economy principles and sustainable packaging initiatives, these biopolymers present innovative solutions to mitigate plastic pollution, reduce food waste, and promote environmental responsibility. This review highlights their potential to catalyze a paradigm shift in the food packaging sector, advancing high-performance, safe, and eco-friendly applications.

Title: Morphological and Mechanical Characterization of Films Incorporating Porphyran Extracted from Porphyra Dioica
Snippet: Despite the identified environmental problems (especially when considering single-use films and coatings for the protection of fast-consumption products), the use of plastics in food packaging is ubiquitous and rising [2], promoted by their low costs and functional advantages over traditional materials (e.g., thermosealability, microwavability) [3]. New packaging systems based on edible, biodegradable, and/or compostable materials have been developed as means of limiting the use of persistent plastics [4]. Biopolymers extracted from plant and animal sources or derived from natural polymers can be used for this purpose [1,2] and have been developed into actual commercial products in the last few years [4]. In particular, polysaccharides from macroalgae (mostly alginates, carrageenans, and agar) are being increasingly used for the formulation of edible packaging, either alone or combined with other biopolymers [4][5][6]. Such packaging can be used in the form of wraps, pouches, and coatings, but despite current technological advances and conversion processes, further progress is still required regarding their poor mechanical and barrier properties [2,4,7]. In this context, the current authors have been developing novel biodegradable edible films based on porphyran extract isolated from the red macroalgae Porphyra dioica [8]. Porphyran is an anionic, water-soluble polysaccharide, with a linear backbone and a very complex structure consisting of repeating arrangements of D-galactose and L-galactosesulfate units in alternating sequence (Figure 1a), disturbed by the partial substitution of D-galactose by methylether (Figure 1b) and of L-galactose-sulphate by anhydrous-Lgalactose (Figure 1c) [7,9]. The proportions of these components vary widely from sample to sample, with those of sulfated ester ranging from 6 to 11% and those of 6-anhydrogalactose from 5 to 19% [10]. [11]. Residues present: (b) methylether and (c) anhydrous-L-galactose [7].

Title: Eco-friendly bioplastic from Pontederia crassipes: cellulose and carboxymethyl cellulose biopolymers for sustainable, biodegradable bioplastic film
Snippet: Expanded usage of polyethylene film in different industries lead to accumulation of plastics in the environment, which cause pollution and toxicity to life forms. It can be replaced by the bioplastics which are biodegradable, biocompatible, eco-friendly, and can be obtained from renewable sources at low cost such as plant weeds. The biopolymer, cellulose can be extracted from aquatic weeds since they are abundantly available from aquatic system, easy and safe to handle, and biocompatible. Pontederia crassipes an aquatic floating weed, widely dispersed in surface of polluted rivers and ponds. Directed to remove from water bodies by EPA due to its negative impacts on aquatic animal life and the collected biomass as such cannot be used as a feed due to the presence of polyphenols and nitrates. In the current study, about 30% of cellulose was extracted by delignification and bleaching of weed biomass collected from a river. Extracted cellulose was converted into another form of derived polymer, known as carboxy methyl cellulose (CMC) by treating with monochloro acetic acid. Biodegradable bioplastic was prepared using gelatin as gelling agent and glycerol as plasticizer by varying concentrations. Properties of the extracted cellulose, CMC, and bioplastic from cellulose and CMC, were analyzed by measuring film thickness, tensile strength, elongation point, FTIR, and antioxidant assay. About 25.7 µm thickness cellulose biofilm exhibited higher tensile strength of 55.3 MPa at dry, 45.5 MPa at wet condition and 24 µg/ml of antioxidant activity was observed. This research highlights the potential of utilizing water hyacinth, a typically problematic weed, to develop sustainable biopolymers that address the growing environmental concerns associated with conventional plastic waste. Thus, this research work provides a potential biological safe approach to prepare bioplastic film for commercial applications. While, gelatin is costly, a suitable, cheap alternative need to be identified to reduce the cost of production of the bioplastic film.  However, further efforts are required to enhance the scalability of the product.

Title: Marine Biopolymers: Applications in Food Packaging
Snippet: Marine sources are gaining popularity and attention as novel materials for manufacturing biopolymers such as proteins and polysaccharides. Due to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and non-toxicity features, these biopolymers have been claimed to be beneficial in the development of food packaging materials. Several studies have thoroughly researched the extraction, isolation, and latent use of marine biopolymers in the fabrication of environmentally acceptable packaging. Thus, a review was designed to provide an overview of (a) the chemical composition, unique properties, and extraction methods of marine biopolymers; (b) the application of marine biopolymers in film and coating development for improved shelf-life of packaged foods; (c) production flaws and proposed solutions for better isolation of marine biopolymers; (d) methods of preparation of edible films and coatings from marine biopolymers; and (e) safety aspects. According to our review, these biopolymers would make a significant component of a biodegradable food packaging system, reducing the amount of plastic packaging used and resulting in considerable environmental and economic benefits.

Title: Antioxidant Molecules from Marine Fungi: Methodologies and Perspectives
Snippet: Microbial polysaccharides, due to their low cost, have emerged as new and industrially important biopolymers competing with natural gums obtained from marine algae and higher plants, for the development of biodegradable, eco-friendly and non-toxic food packaging films, among other application [239]. Marine fungi, as described in this review, have shown the ability to produce plenty of polysaccharides with antioxidant properties. Therefore, these polymers represent promising candidate for the development of biodegradable active packaging material.

Snippet: Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth) has several advantages, making it a promising reinforcing material for starch-based bioplastics. The relatively low lignin content (often below 15%) facilitates pretreatment and improves compatibility in the polymer matrix [3]. In addition, this plant grows rapidly, produces high biomass throughout the year, and is abundant in tropical aquatic ecosystems, making it a cheap and sustainable source of raw material [7]. The use of water hyacinth provides a renewable source of cellulose and contributes to environmental management by reducing the negative impact of this invasive species on freshwater ecosystems. 

In this study, bioplastic film was developed using sweet potato flour as the main polymer matrix reinforced with water hyacinth cellulose. Water hyacinth cellulose was obtained through delignification and bleaching methods. Snippet: Plastics are a menacing threat to the environment. As a substitute for synthetic plastics, biodegradable alternatives can mitigate the pollution problem.
